name: LuaJIT Remake (LJR)
baseline: PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter (official Lua); also compared against the LuaJIT interpreter
workload: Run time of the Lua benchmark programs in the repo's luabench directory (about 50 files: binary-trees, fannkuch, nbody, richards, deltablue, scimark, ray, spectral-norm, ...), interpreter only (JIT tiers not implemented yet), geometric mean over benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: 'our interpreter is 34.6% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter, and 185% faster than the official PUC Lua5.1 interpreter' (geometric average over all benchmarks, each repeated 5 times)
compiler_and_flags: Built with `python3 ljr-build make release` inside Docker; compiler and flags not stated in the README (build script not inspected). run_bench.sh pins the process with taskset and sleeps 3 s between runs.
tradeoffs: x86-64 Linux only; Lua 5.1 semantics only; interpreter and baseline JIT are generated from a bytecode semantic description by the author's Deegen meta-compiler; tables use hidden classes instead of Lua's hash tables; package library (require/module) not implemented.
caveats: Garbage collector is not implemented; for 'fair' comparison the author turned GC off in the other Lua implementations as well, so allocation-heavy results exclude GC cost. Numbers come from the author's laptop (author notes up to 10% thermal fluctuation), compiler and flags not stated, so first-party tier C. 'N% faster' wording is ambiguous (185% faster is about 2.85x if read as speed ratio; the 2022 blog said 171% / almost 3x). Per-benchmark chart is an image; the repo's JIT tiers were still being written (latest commits are DFG backend work). Blog posts with details are on github.io and were not reachable here.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ interpreter faster than CPython Lua benchmark github' surfaced the author's blog 'Building the fastest Lua interpreter.. automatically!'; opened the github.com repo, its README, run_bench.sh, luabench listing and commit feed.

name: Wren
baseline: Lua 5.2.3, Python 3.3.4, Ruby 2.0.0p247 (also Python 2.7.5 and LuaJIT 2.0.2 with JIT off)
workload: Four small benchmarks (method call, DeltaBlue, binary trees, recursive Fibonacci); best of 10 runs, interpreter startup excluded.
claimed_speedup: Method call: wren 0.12s vs lua 0.35s, ruby 0.20s, python3 0.78s. DeltaBlue: wren 0.13s vs python3 0.48s. Binary trees: wren 0.22s vs lua 0.52s, python3 0.38s, ruby 0.24s. Recursive Fibonacci: wren 0.20s vs lua 0.28s, ruby 0.22s, python3 0.57s. (LuaJIT with JIT off is faster on binary trees 0.11s and fib 0.10s.)
hardware: MacBook Pro, 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7, 16 GB 1,600 MHz DDR3 (author's laptop)
tradeoffs: Small class-based language (VM under 4,000 lines); NaN-tagged values, fixed object layout, copy-down inheritance; classes cannot be modified at runtime; compiles as C99 or C++98 and later, embeddable through a C API.
caveats: Numbers are from the early 2010s (Lua 5.2.3, Python 3.3.4, Ruby 2.0.0, DDR3 laptop) and have not been refreshed; modern CPython 3.11+ and Lua 5.4 are faster. Only four microbenchmarks; the author states most benchmarks 'aren't worth the pixels they're printed on'. Wren loses to LuaJIT in interpreter-only mode on binary trees and fib. Compiler and flags not stated. The benchmark harness is in the repo (test/benchmark) but was not opened.
found_via: WebSearch 'github scripting language virtual machine README benchmarks faster than Lua faster than Python' listed wren.io/performance; wren.io is blocked here, so read doc/site/performance.markdown from the wren-lang/wren repo and opened the github.com repo page and commit feed.

name: Codon
workload: kostya/jit-benchmarks: single-threaded Benchmarks Game style programs run as the same Python source (CPython interpreter vs `codon build --release` native executable); time measured inside the program, so Codon compile time is excluded.
claimed_speedup: Best time (s), CPython vs Codon: binarytrees 73.15 vs 1.0; mandelbrot 37.52 vs 0.65; matmul 22.73 vs 0.25; nbody 53.72 vs 2.23; spectralnorm 20.69 vs 0.53; fasta 8.65 vs 1.66; fannkuchredux 4.04 vs 1.82; knucleotide 8.41 vs 2.69; brainfuck > 190 vs 2.05; brainfuck2 142.26 vs 1.91 (ratios derived from page data: about 73x, 58x, 91x, 24x, 39x, 5.2x, 2.2x, 3.1x, over 90x, 74x).
compiler_and_flags: Codon 0.15.5 built with `codon build --release -o <out> test.py` (tools/languages.rb); CPython 3.10.7 in Docker on Ubuntu 22.10.
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler for a Python subset, not a drop-in CPython replacement: static typing, fixed-width ints, different semantics for some features; imports CPython modules through a bridge; native multithreading (no GIL), OpenMP and GPU support; compiler is written in C++ on LLVM.
caveats: Third-party suite dates from 2023-02-28 (round 1, Codon 0.15.5); pidigits, regexdna and revcomp did not compile or run under Codon (shown as '-'). It is a compiler, so compile times (4 to 7 s in the suite) are extra and speedups apply only to code in the supported subset. First-party README separately claims fib(40) 17.98 s on CPython vs 0.276 s on Codon and 'typical speedups ... 10-100x' (hardware not stated); not used for the tier. Compiler is C++ but the product is a standalone Python-language toolchain rather than a C++ library.
found_via: WebSearch 'Python interpreter written in C++ faster than CPython benchmarks github' surfaced kostya/jit-benchmarks; opened github.com/exaloop/codon (README, LICENSE, commit feed) and the kostya README, tools/languages.rb and docker/codon.

name: mypyc
workload: kostya/jit-benchmarks: the same unannotated Python benchmark source run on CPython and after `mypyc test.py` (compiled to a C extension).
claimed_speedup: Best time (s), CPython vs mypyc: binarytrees 73.15 vs 23.25; brainfuck > 190 vs 93.55; brainfuck2 142.26 vs 77.25; fannkuchredux 4.04 vs 2.74; fasta 8.65 vs 6.44; mandelbrot 37.52 vs 23.26 (ratios derived from page data: 3.1x, over 2.0x, 1.8x, 1.5x, 1.3x, 1.6x). Not faster on matmul (22.73 vs 24.95) or pidigits (6.17 vs 6.2).
compiler_and_flags: mypyc 1.0.1, `mypyc test.py` (tools/languages.rb), CPython 3.10.7 in Docker on Ubuntu 22.10.
stars_or_usage: 20.7k stars (python/mypy; mypyc lives in the mypyc/ directory)
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiles type-annotated Python modules to C extensions that run on top of CPython (all third-party libraries keep working); some Python dynamism is not supported (see mypyc differences_from_python docs); needs a C compiler at build time.
caveats: Benchmark sources in the third-party suite carry no type annotations, so the numbers understate what annotated code gets; the suite is from 2023-02-28 (mypyc 1.0.1). The nbody row shows 0.0 s with 1 run (invalid) and knucleotide and revcomp show no result. First-party docs (mypyc/doc/introduction.rst) say 'Existing code with type annotations is often 1.5x to 5x faster when compiled. Code tuned for mypyc can be 5x to 10x faster' and the mypy README says the compiled mypy is about 4x faster; those were not measured here. The language is Python (a compiler emitting C), not usable directly from C++.
found_via: Harvested from kostya/jit-benchmarks (found via WebSearch 'Python interpreter written in C++ faster than CPython benchmarks github'); opened mypyc/doc/introduction.rst and the python/mypy repo page and commit feed.

name: Pyston
claimed_speedup: Pyston 'full' (CPython 3.8.12 fork with DynASM JIT): 'roughly 30% faster than CPython on web serving macrobenchmarks'; Pyston 'lite' (JIT extension module): 'roughly 10% faster on macrobenchmarks'.
tradeoffs: Pyston-full is a CPython 3.8.12 fork with a very-low-overhead JIT (DynASM), quickening, attribute caching and build-process improvements (PGO/BOLT); API compatible but not ABI compatible, so C extensions need recompiling; pyston-lite is a pip-installable JIT extension for CPython 3.7 to 3.10 that stays binary compatible.
caveats: First-party claim without hardware, compiler or per-benchmark numbers; the blog with details (blog.pyston.org) was not reachable. The gains are measured against CPython 3.8-3.10, which predates the adaptive specializing interpreter in CPython 3.11+, so the advantage is likely obsolete. The repo page marks the project as no longer maintained; last commit seen in the feed was 2024-08-12. License is the CPython PSF license (the LICENSE file begins with the Python history text).
found_via: WebSearch 'Python-compatible interpreter OR JIT OR compiler faster than CPython' returned the Pyston README summary; opened github.com/pyston/pyston, its raw README, LICENSE and commit feed, and the pyston/python-macrobenchmarks page.

name: LuaAOT 5.4 (luaot)
workload: Seven Benchmarks Game style Lua programs (binarytrees, fannkuch, fasta, knucleotide, mandelbrot, nbody, spectralnorm), 20 timed runs each; Lua bytecode compiled ahead of time to C and loaded as a .so module vs the stock interpreter.
claimed_speedup: README: 'For numerical benchmarks it can be twice as fast as regular Lua. But overall, it is not as fast as LuaJIT or Pallene.' Median wall time (s) from statistics/times-slow.txt, lua vs cor (the LuaAOT column per statistics/plot.r): binarytrees 3.51 vs 2.67; fannkuch 44.33 vs 21.9; fasta 5.04 vs 3.82; knucleotide 4.13 vs 3.44; mandelbrot 16.28 vs 6.16; nbody 17.76 vs 12.17; spectralnorm 39.83 vs 18.92 (ratios derived from page data: 1.31x, 2.02x, 1.32x, 1.20x, 2.64x, 1.46x, 2.11x).
compiler_and_flags: Generated C compiled with `gcc -shared -fPIC -O2 -g` (scripts/compile); Lua built with `make guess`; gcc version not stated.
tradeoffs: Modified Lua 5.4.3 with a Lua-bytecode-to-C compiler (luaot) that converts jumps to gotos and removes dispatch overhead; compiled modules need a C compiler and the modified Lua headers; one executable or .so per Lua module.
caveats: Hardware and CPU model are not stated in the files I opened (the README refers to a paper whose text I could not reach), so tier C although the raw timing data and scripts are public. Which column is LuaAOT was inferred from statistics/plot.r (impl_used lua, trm, cor, jit mapped to 'Lua', 'Trampoline', 'LuaAOT', 'LuaJIT'); the separate 'aot' column gives similar ratios (1.23x to 2.25x). Only seven benchmarks, mostly numeric; it is an AOT compiler rather than an interpreter, so it does not speed up code loaded at runtime. Upstream is Lua 5.4.3; GitHub fork status not checked.
found_via: WebSearch 'Lua 5.4 compatible interpreter faster than PUC Lua benchmark github C++ OR C' surfaced hugomg/lua-aot-5.4; opened the repo page, README, experiments and statistics directories, times-slow.txt, plot.r, scripts/compile and the commit feed.

name: Shed Skin
workload: Over 80 non-trivial programs in the repo's examples directory (over 25,000 lines), plus a 'sieve' example with n=100000000 compared with CPython, Nuitka, PyPy and Numba.
claimed_speedup: 'a typical speedup of 1-100 times over CPython 3.14 (average 20 times, median 12 times)'; sieve (n=100000000): cpython 3.10.6 13.4 s, cpython 3.11.0 11.4 s, nuitka 0.6.16 11.4 s, pypy 3.9.12 5.8 s, numba 0.56.4 2.5 s, shedskin 0.9.9 1.9 s (--int32), 1.8 s (--int32 --nowrap --nobounds).
compiler_and_flags: shedskin 0.9.9 with --int32 (and --nowrap --nobounds for the fastest row); C++ compiler and flags not stated.
license: GPL-3.0 (compiler); Expat (MIT-style) for the C++ runtime library under shedskin/lib; BSD-3-Clause and BSL-1.0 for a few bundled files
tradeoffs: Transpiles a restricted, implicitly statically typed subset of Python 3 to C++ (no nested functions, no variable-length argument lists, about 25 supported stdlib modules, no external libraries); programs may need substantial refactoring; Python-written compiler, C++ output.
caveats: First-party numbers with no hardware or compiler flags; the speedup chart for the 80 programs is an image (perf_comp.png, git tag 'performance_comparison' measured against CPython 3.10) and was not inspected; the README text quotes CPython 3.14 for the headline. The sieve row uses the narrower int32 type, which the README itself says Numba would match if it used int32 (now both default to int64). Not usable as a drop-in interpreter. Licenses are split (GPL-3.0 compiler, Expat runtime library that generated code links against); all are OSI-approved.
found_via: WebSearch 'Python ahead-of-time compiler C++ faster than CPython github Shed Skin OR Pythran OR Codon' and github.com/topics/python-implementation; opened the repo page, README, LICENSE and commit feed.

name: pocketpy
workload: 'primes' benchmark (benchmarks/primes.py) run on pkpy 1.2.7, CPython 3.8.10, Lua 5.3.3 and a C++ version.
claimed_speedup: primes benchmark: c++ 0.104s, lua 5.3.3 1.576s, pkpy 1.2.7 2.385s, cpython 3.8.10 2.871s (pkpy about 1.2x faster than CPython 3.8.10, derived from page data); README says 'Currently, pkpy is as fast as cpython 3.9.'
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the Python and Lua rows (C++ row built as gnu++11).
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars; used in TIC-80, godot-pocketpy and others
tradeoffs: Portable Python 3 interpreter in C11 designed as a game-scripting alternative to Lua; single-header or CMake integration; supports a subset of Python (no full standard library); tested on Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS, Emscripten and Raspberry Pi OS.
caveats: One micro-benchmark whose table is for version 1.2.7 (the repo is now at a later major version); Lua 5.3.3 is about 1.5x faster than pkpy in the same table; CPython 3.8.10 is old (3.11+ is much faster); compiler and flags missing so the tier is C even though benchmark files are linked at a commit. WSL results. The linked performance page (pocketpy.github.io) is blocked here.
found_via: Checked as a known Python-in-C interpreter candidate (not returned by WebSearch); opened github.com/pocketpy/pocketpy, its raw README and commit feed.

name: Dino
baseline: Python 3.4.x and Ruby 2.1.x (also PyPy 2.2.x, SpiderMonkey 1.8.x, Scala 2.10.x, OCaml 4.0.x)
workload: Old computer-language-shootout style programs (loop, hash, fact, fib, exceptions, method calls, object creation, sieve, sort, statistics, random, threads, startup, compile) on x86-64, AARCH64, ARM and PPC64; times are relative to Dino's best result = 1.0.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 (relative times, Dino best = 1.0; plain Dino without hints / Python / Ruby): Loop 19 / 257 / 157; Fact 13.2 / 90.4 / 25.2; Fib 112 / 492 / 142; Method 1.0 / 5.8 / 1.5; Object 1.0 / 4.4 / 1.4; Sieve 1.0 / 37.9 / 4.5; Thread 1.0 / 125 / 43.6; Start 1.0 / 10.9 / 29.4; Hash 1.0 / 2.4 / 2.2. PyPy is faster than Dino on loop, fact and fib.
hardware: x86-64 i5-4670 3.4 GHz Haswell; also AARCH64 (X-Gene), ARM (Exynos 5410 1.6 GHz Cortex-A15), PPC64 (3.5 GHz Power7)
license: GPL-2.0 and LGPL-2.0 (as shown on the GitHub page; exact SPDX variant not verified)
tradeoffs: Dynamically typed scripting language with an optimizing bytecode interpreter, mark-and-sweep plus mark-and-copy GC, optional function-level JIT through C code generation, type inference, fibers and a C FFI; its own language, not source compatible with Python or Ruby.
caveats: Results are from a 2016 document (version 0.98 development) on Python 3.4 and Ruby 2.1; on AARCH64 Python 2.7.5 was used because Python 3 was absent, and there Python is faster on the hash benchmark (0.5 vs 1.7). Dino's best row uses JIT, pure-function and inline hints; the plain row is quoted here. Table is in the repo's README.md document (readable as a slide deck), numbers are relative rather than seconds, compiler flags not stated. Author is a GCC maintainer; repo is dormant since 2019.
found_via: Recalled Vladimir Makarov's Dino (he also wrote MIR, which is already catalogued) while checking interpreter READMEs; opened github.com/dino-lang/dino, its raw README.md and commit feed.

name: Luau
workload: No benchmark in the repo README; the project says its runtime is a heavily modified Lua 5.1 runtime with a rewritten interpreter.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'Luau is largely implemented from scratch, with the language runtime being a very heavily modified version of Lua 5.1 runtime, with completely rewritten interpreter and other performance innovations.' (A performance page at luau.org says it is noticeably faster than Lua 5.x; that site was not reachable here.)
stars_or_usage: 5.9k stars; used by Roblox, Alan Wake 2, Farming Simulator 2025, Second Life, Warframe
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1 compatible with a gradual type system, sandboxing, a multi-pass compiler and optional native code generation; not fully compatible with Lua 5.2 to 5.4 features.
caveats: Tier D: no numbers on any page I opened. The repo has a bench/ directory (bench.py, micro_tests, tests) that could be run to produce a measured claim; luau.org/performance and the vegorov-rbx.github.io mirror are blocked here, and search snippets say it is 'noticeably faster than Lua 5.x' and close to the LuaJIT interpreter on some workloads, which I could not verify.

name: GraalPy
workload: Python Performance Benchmark Suite (pyperformance), geometric-mean speedup over CPython, both interpreters installed through pyenv and run with `pip install pyperformance && pyperformance run`.
claimed_speedup: 'GraalPy is geomean ~4x faster than CPython on the official Python Performance Benchmark Suite'; chart data: CPython 3.12.8 = 1, GraalPy 25.1.3 = 4.30 (geomean speedup over CPython).
compiler_and_flags: GraalPy 25.1.3 vs CPython 3.12.8, both installed via pyenv; build flags of CPython not stated.
tradeoffs: Python 3.13-compliant runtime on the JVM (GraalVM Truffle); JIT warm-up time and larger memory footprint; native C extension support is experimental (README: near CPython speed for extensions, varies by workload); embeds in Java and can produce native images.
caveats: First-party claim; hardware, JVM settings, warm-up policy and per-benchmark results are not on the README page (only the bar chart SVG, whose data I read). Geomean over pyperformance includes warmed-up peak numbers, so startup-dominated scripts will not see the gain. Java implementation, not usable directly from C++ (embedding goes through the GraalVM polyglot API); lies at the edge of the language-interpreters and JIT categories.
found_via: Checked READMEs of alternative Python implementations (GraalPy was not returned by WebSearch); opened github.com/oracle/graalpython, its raw README, docs/user/assets/performance.svg and the commit feed.

name: KPHP
baseline: PHP 7.4 with OpCache (Zend micro_bench.php and bench.php); PHP 7.2 for the vk.com page timings
workload: php-src Zend/micro_bench.php and Zend/bench.php (after removing a couple of tests that do not compile), 5 runs each; plus vk.com page generation times and ML-style kernels measured by the authors.
claimed_speedup: micro_bench avg 3.297 s on PHP 7.4 vs 0.460 s on KPHP; bench avg 0.659 s vs 0.119 s ('KPHP is found to be 5-7 times faster'); vk.com/feed 10.1 s vs 0.95 s, vk.com/im 1.25 s vs 0.46 s, vk.com/ads 0.73 s vs 0.20 s (PHP 7.2); neural networks with huge matrices ~8 s vs 0.24 s; deep decision trees ~5 s vs 0.14 s; README: 'when your code fits best practices, it runs 3-10 times faster than PHP'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (PHP 7.4 with OpCache and without XDebug; KPHP compiler version and C++ flags not given).
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler from a limited, strictly typed PHP subset to C++ and then a native binary; no generators, anonymous classes, SPL or XML parsing, no call-by-name; existing PHP code usually needs rewriting to compile; the runtime is C++ and has a fast FFI.
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model or compiler flags. The doc itself marks the Zend micro benchmarks as 'absolutely synthetic' and warns it is wrong to say KPHP is always faster (code dominated by C-implemented PHP functions such as strpos or parse_url gains almost nothing). Baseline is PHP 7.4/7.2, far behind PHP 8 with its JIT, so today's gap is probably smaller. vk.com page timings and ML kernels are not reproducible from public code. The project website is on github.io (blocked here); the benchmark page was read from the docs/ directory of the repo.
found_via: Recalled PHP-to-C++ compilers while checking dynamic-language implementations; opened github.com/VKCOM/kphp, its raw README, docs/kphp-language/kphp-vs-php/benchmarks.md and the commit feed.
